# Before proceedings {#sec-dr-preaction}

> *Assessment objective 3: pre-action considerations and steps.*

## Limitation

Limitation is the first thing a litigator checks and the last thing they can fix. It is examined by
calculation, so learn the period, the trigger date, and the exceptions.

### The periods

| Claim | Period | Runs from | Provision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simple contract** | **6 years** | The date of **breach** | s.5 Limitation Act 1980 |
| Contract under **deed** (specialty) | **12 years** | The date of breach | s.8 |
| **Tort** generally | **6 years** | The date the cause of action **accrued** — for negligence, when **damage** is suffered | s.2 |
| **Negligence** causing latent damage (not personal injury) | 6 years from accrual **or** **3 years** from the **starting date**, whichever expires **later** — subject to a **15-year longstop** | Knowledge of the material facts about the damage | ss.14A, 14B |
| **Personal injury** | **3 years** | The later of the date of **accrual** and the claimant's **date of knowledge** | ss.11, 14 |
| **Fatal accidents** | **3 years** | The later of the date of **death** and the dependant's date of knowledge | s.12 |
| **Defective products** (Consumer Protection Act 1987) | **3 years**, with a **10-year longstop** from when the product was put into circulation | Damage or knowledge | s.11A |
| **Contribution** between wrongdoers | **2 years** | The judgment or settlement fixing the liability to be contributed to | s.10 |
| Recovery of **land** | 12 years | Accrual | s.15 |

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
For a **contract** claim, time runs from the **breach** — not from when the claimant discovered it, and
not from when the loss was suffered. For a **tort** claim in negligence, time runs from when **damage
occurs**, which may be much later than the negligent act. A question that gives you a negligently
drafted document, a breach years later, and damage later still is testing exactly this: the contract
claim may be statute-barred while the tortious claim is alive.
:::

### Knowledge, and the extensions

**Date of knowledge** (s.14) for a personal injury claim: the date on which the claimant first knew
that the injury was **significant**, that it was **attributable** in whole or in part to the act or
omission alleged to constitute negligence, and the **identity of the defendant**. Knowledge includes
what the claimant might reasonably have been expected to acquire, including from expert advice it was
reasonable to seek. Knowledge that, as a matter of law, the act amounted to negligence is **irrelevant**.

**Section 14A** applies the same idea to other negligence claims: the claimant gets the longer of six
years from accrual, or three years from the date they had both the knowledge required to bring the
action and the right to bring it — subject to the absolute **15-year longstop** in s.14B, which runs
from the negligent act or omission and applies even if the claimant never had knowledge.

**Section 28 — disability.** If the claimant was a **child** or **lacked capacity** *when the cause of
action accrued*, time does not begin to run until the disability ends: a child's period therefore runs
from their **18th birthday**, so a child injured at seven has until their 21st birthday to bring a
personal injury claim. Supervening disability does **not** stop the clock.

**Section 32 — fraud, concealment and mistake.** Where the action is based on the defendant's fraud,
where a fact relevant to the claimant's right of action has been **deliberately concealed** by the
defendant, or where the action is for relief from the consequences of a **mistake**, time does not
begin to run until the claimant has **discovered** the fraud, concealment or mistake, or **could with
reasonable diligence have discovered** it.

**Sections 29–31 — acknowledgment and part payment.** In a claim for a debt or other liquidated sum, a
written, signed **acknowledgment** of the debt, or a **part payment**, restarts the six-year clock — but
cannot revive a claim already statute-barred.

**Section 33 — the discretion.** In **personal injury and fatal accident** claims only, the court has an
equitable discretion to **disapply** the primary limitation period where it is equitable to do so,
having regard to the prejudice to each party and to the s.33(3) factors: the length of and reasons for
the delay, the effect of the delay on the **cogency of the evidence**, the defendant's conduct after
the cause of action arose, the duration of any disability, how promptly the claimant acted once they
knew, and the steps the claimant took to obtain advice.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Section 33 is confined to personal injury and fatal accident claims. There is **no** general judicial
discretion to extend limitation in a contract or property claim, however sympathetic the facts. An
option offering the court a discretion to disapply the six-year contract period is always wrong.
:::

### How limitation operates

- It is a **procedural** defence. It bars the **remedy**, not the right, and it must be **pleaded** in
  the defence — the court will not take the point of its own motion. (Conversion under s.3 and land
  under s.17 are the exceptions, where title is extinguished.)
- The claim is **brought** when the claim form is **received by the court office**, not when it is
  sealed. Practice Direction 7A says so, and a claim form delivered on the last day is in time even if
  it is issued days later.
- If the period is about to expire and the pre-action protocol has not been complied with, the
  claimant should **issue** to protect the position and then invite the court to **stay** the
  proceedings so that the protocol steps can be completed.
- Parties may agree a **standstill agreement** to suspend time while they negotiate. Draft it
  carefully: an agreement that merely says the parties "will not take a limitation point" is a
  contractual promise, not an extension.

## Practice Direction – Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols

Where no approved protocol covers the dispute, the **Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and
Protocols** applies. Its aims (para 3) are that the parties should:

- **understand each other's position**;
- make **decisions** about how to proceed;
- try to **settle** the issues without proceedings;
- consider a form of **ADR**;
- support the **efficient management** of proceedings; and
- **reduce the costs** of resolving the dispute.

### The steps

Paragraph 6 sets out what the parties should do where no protocol applies:

1. The **claimant** writes to the defendant with **concise details** of the claim — the basis on which
   it is made, a summary of the facts, what the claimant wants from the defendant, and, if money, how
   the amount is calculated.
2. The **defendant** responds within a **reasonable time** — 14 days in a straightforward case, and no
   more than three months in a very complex one — saying whether the claim is accepted and, if not,
   the reasons, together with an explanation of which facts and parts of the claim are disputed and
   whether the defendant is making a counterclaim.
3. The parties **disclose key documents** relevant to the issues in dispute.
4. The parties **consider ADR**.

Paragraph 4 imposes **proportionality**: the steps taken must be proportionate, and the Practice
Direction must not be used as a tactical device to generate costs or to gain an unfair advantage.

### ADR and the last resort principle

Litigation is a **last resort** (para 8). The parties should consider whether negotiation or another
form of ADR might enable them to settle, and the court **may require evidence** that the parties
considered it. **Silence** in response to an invitation to participate may itself be unreasonable and
may lead to a costs sanction.

### Non-compliance and its consequences

The court will look at whether the parties have complied **in substance**; minor or technical failures
are not penalised. Where there has been a significant failure, the court may:

- **stay** the proceedings while the missed steps are taken;
- order the party at fault to **pay costs**, in whole or in part;
- order those costs on the **indemnity basis**;
- if the party at fault is a **claimant** who has been awarded a sum of money, deprive it of **interest**
  or award interest at a lower rate;
- if the party at fault is a **defendant** ordered to pay a sum of money, award **interest** at a rate
  up to **10% above base rate**.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Failure to comply with a protocol does **not** invalidate the claim, and it is not a ground for
striking out. The sanctions are about **costs and interest**, and occasionally a stay. An option saying
the claim will be struck out because the claimant did not send a letter before claim is wrong.
:::

### The approved protocols

Where an approved protocol applies, it displaces the Practice Direction's generic steps. Those most
likely to appear:

| Protocol | Distinctive features |
|---|---|
| **Personal Injury** | Letter of claim in two copies (one for insurers); defendant has 21 days to acknowledge and **3 months** thereafter to investigate and state whether liability is admitted; agreed expert procedure with the claimant nominating names |
| **Debt Claims** | Applies where a **business** claims from an **individual**. Letter of claim with an information sheet, reply form and financial statement; the debtor has **30 days** to respond; a further 30 days if documents are requested; the creditor must give **14 days'** notice before issuing |
| **Professional Negligence** | Preliminary notice; letter of claim; the professional has **21 days** to acknowledge and **3 months** to investigate and provide a letter of response and/or settlement |
| **Construction and Engineering** | Letter of claim, response, and a **pre-action meeting** |
| **Clinical Disputes** | Request for records; letter of claim; **4 months** to respond |

Each shares a common shape — letter of claim, acknowledgment, substantive response, disclosure of key
documents, consideration of ADR — and each attaches its own timetable. The **structure** is examinable;
the individual timetables less so, except for the debt claims protocol, which is distinctive because it
protects consumers.

## Applicable law

Which country's law governs the dispute is decided by **assimilated** versions of the Rome I and Rome II
Regulations, which continue to apply in England and Wales after Brexit.

### Contract: Rome I

**Article 3 — party choice.** The contract is governed by the law chosen by the parties. The choice
must be **express or clearly demonstrated** by the terms or the circumstances. Parties may choose the
law for the whole or part of the contract, and may change it.

**Article 4 — no choice.** A cascade:

1. **Specific rules** by contract type:

   | Contract | Governing law |
   |---|---|
   | Sale of **goods** | The **seller's** habitual residence |
   | Provision of **services** | The **service provider's** habitual residence |
   | A right *in rem* in, or a tenancy of, **immovable property** | Where the property is **situated** |
   | **Franchise** | The **franchisee's** habitual residence |
   | **Distribution** | The **distributor's** habitual residence |
   | Sale of goods by **auction** | Where the auction takes place |

2. Otherwise, or where the contract falls into more than one category: the law of the country where the
   party required to effect the **characteristic performance** has their habitual residence.
3. **Escape clause** (Art 4(3)): if it is clear from all the circumstances that the contract is
   **manifestly more closely connected** with another country, that country's law applies.
4. Failing all of that (Art 4(4)): the law of the country with which it is **most closely connected**.

**Protective rules.** Article 6 (consumer contracts) and Article 8 (individual employment contracts)
provide that a choice of law cannot deprive the consumer of the protection of the mandatory rules of
their habitual residence, or the employee of the mandatory rules of the country where they habitually
work. **Article 9** preserves the **overriding mandatory provisions** of the forum, and **Article 21**
allows the court to refuse to apply a foreign rule that is manifestly incompatible with public policy.

For a company, "habitual residence" means its **place of central administration**; for a person acting
in the course of business, their **principal place of business**.

### Tort: Rome II

**Article 4(1) — the general rule.** The applicable law is that of the country in which the **damage
occurs**, irrespective of the country in which the **event giving rise** to the damage occurred, and
irrespective of the countries in which the **indirect consequences** of that event occur.

**Article 4(2).** If, at the time the damage occurs, both the person claimed to be liable and the person
sustaining damage have their **habitual residence in the same country**, the law of that country
applies instead.

**Article 4(3) — escape clause.** If the tort is **manifestly more closely connected** with another
country, that country's law applies. A **pre-existing relationship** between the parties, such as a
contract, is expressly identified as capable of establishing that connection.

**Article 14 — choice.** The parties may choose the applicable law: **after** the event giving rise to
the damage, or **before** it if all the parties are pursuing a commercial activity and the agreement is
freely negotiated.

**Special regimes**: product liability (Art 5, a cascade), unfair competition (Art 6), environmental
damage (Art 7, where the claimant may elect for the law of the country in which the event occurred),
and intellectual property (Art 8, the law of the country for which protection is claimed, with **no**
freedom to choose).

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Article 4(1) is counter-intuitive and reliably tested. The law is that of the place where the **damage**
occurs, **not** where the wrongful act was committed. A defective component made negligently in France
and fitted to a machine that injures a worker in England produces **English** law under Art 4(1) —
unless Art 4(2) or Art 4(3) displaces it. Note also that Rome II **excludes defamation and privacy**,
for which the common law rules apply.
:::

## Jurisdiction

Since the end of the transition period the **Brussels Recast Regulation** no longer applies to
proceedings commenced in England and Wales. Three regimes now matter.

### Hague 2005 — exclusive choice of court agreements

Where a contract contains an **exclusive** jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of a contracting
state, the **2005 Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements** requires the chosen court to hear
the case and other contracting states to decline. The contracting parties include the EU, the UK,
Mexico, Singapore and Montenegro. The Convention does not cover **asymmetric** (one-sided) clauses on
the prevailing view, and does not cover non-exclusive clauses.

### Hague 2019 — recognition and enforcement

The **2019 Hague Judgments Convention** entered into force for the **United Kingdom on 1 July 2025**,
applying to judgments arising out of proceedings **issued on or after** that date. It provides a
treaty basis for the recognition and enforcement of judgments between contracting states — the EU,
Ukraine, Uruguay, Albania and Montenegro among them — and is significantly wider than Hague 2005
because it is not confined to exclusive jurisdiction clauses.

### The common law rules

Where neither Convention applies, the English court's jurisdiction depends on **service**.

**Defendant within the jurisdiction.** Service of the claim form on a defendant present in England and
Wales founds jurisdiction **as of right**. The defendant's remedy is to apply for a **stay** on the
ground of *forum non conveniens*.

*Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd* [1987] AC 460 supplies the test: the court will stay
proceedings if the defendant shows that there is **another available forum which is clearly or
distinctly more appropriate** — the "natural forum", with which the action has the **most real and
substantial connection**. The burden then shifts to the claimant to show that justice nevertheless
requires the trial to take place in England.

**Defendant outside the jurisdiction.** The claimant needs the court's **permission** to serve out
(CPR 6.36), unless one of the exceptions in CPR 6.32–6.33 applies — most importantly where the contract
contains a term to the effect that the English court shall have jurisdiction, or where jurisdiction
arises under Hague 2005.

To obtain permission, the claimant must establish three things:

1. A **good arguable case** that the claim falls within one of the **gateways** in Practice Direction
   6B, paragraph 3.1;
2. A **serious issue to be tried** on the merits — a real prospect of success; and
3. That **England is the proper place** in which to bring the claim (*forum conveniens*).

The gateways most often examined:

| Category | Gateway |
|---|---|
| General | The defendant is **domiciled** within the jurisdiction; a claim for an **injunction** ordering the defendant to do or refrain from doing an act within the jurisdiction; the defendant is a **necessary or proper party** to a claim against another defendant |
| **Contract** | The contract was **made within** the jurisdiction; made **by or through an agent** within the jurisdiction; is **governed by English law**; contains a term conferring **English jurisdiction**; or the **breach** was committed within the jurisdiction |
| **Tort** | **Damage** was or will be **sustained** within the jurisdiction; or the damage results from an **act committed**, or likely to be committed, within the jurisdiction |

*FS Cairo (Nile Plaza) LLC v Brownlie* [2021] UKSC 45 confirmed that "damage" in the tort gateway bears
its ordinary meaning and covers any **significant** damage sustained in England — including continuing
pain and financial loss suffered here after an accident abroad. The gateway is broad; the real filter is
the third requirement, *forum conveniens*.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Keep the three limbs separate. Satisfying a gateway is **not** enough: the claimant must also show a
serious issue to be tried and that England is the **proper place**. And keep jurisdiction separate from
**applicable law** — an English court can and often does apply foreign law, so the fact that French law
governs a contract does not deprive the English court of jurisdiction.
:::

## Where to start proceedings

### High Court or County Court

Practice Direction 7A allocates business between them:

| Claim | Where it may be started |
|---|---|
| Money claim (not personal injury) of **£100,000 or less** | **County Court only** |
| Money claim of **more than £100,000** | County Court or High Court |
| **Personal injury** claim worth **less than £50,000** | **County Court only** |
| **Personal injury** claim worth **£50,000 or more** | County Court or High Court |

A claimant issuing in the High Court must state in the claim form that it expects to recover more than
£100,000 (or, for personal injury, £50,000 or more), or that an enactment requires the claim to be
started in the High Court, or that the claim is to proceed in a specialist High Court list.

Beyond value, the factors pointing to the High Court are the **financial value and amount in dispute**,
the **complexity** of the facts, legal issues, remedies or procedures, and the **importance** of the
outcome to the public in general.

A case started in the wrong court is not a nullity: the court may **transfer** it (ss.40–42 County
Courts Act 1984), and may penalise the claimant in **costs** for starting in the High Court
unnecessarily.

### The divisions and the specialist courts

The High Court has three divisions: the **King's Bench Division** (contract and tort, including most
commercial disputes and personal injury), the **Chancery Division** (business, property, trusts, land,
intellectual property, companies and insolvency), and the **Family Division**.

The **Business and Property Courts** are an umbrella for the specialist lists:

| Court or list | Business |
|---|---|
| **Commercial Court** (KBD) | National and international commercial disputes — sale of goods, insurance, banking, shipping |
| **Circuit Commercial Courts** | Commercial claims of lower value, outside London |
| **Technology and Construction Court** (KBD) | Building and engineering disputes, professional negligence against construction professionals, IT disputes |
| **Admiralty Court** (KBD) | Shipping, collisions, salvage |
| **Financial List** | Financial markets claims of £50 million or more, or requiring market expertise |
| **Intellectual Property Enterprise Court** (Chancery) | Lower-value IP claims, with a **£500,000** damages cap and recoverable costs capped at **£60,000** on liability and £30,000 on quantum |
| Companies, Insolvency, Competition, Property, Trusts, Revenue lists | As their names suggest |

## The solicitor's position

**Advising on limitation.** A missed limitation period is the archetypal negligence claim against a
litigation solicitor. The date must be calculated and diarised at the outset, and where it is close the
right course is to **issue protectively** rather than to complete the protocol.

**Not taking unfair advantage.** A solicitor must not take unfair advantage of a third party, which
constrains the tone and content of a letter before claim to a litigant in person: threatening
consequences that cannot follow, or asserting a claim known to be bad, breaches the Code of Conduct.
The **SRA warning notice on SLAPPs** — strategic lawsuits against public participation — is expressly
flagged in the assessment specification, and identifies aggressive pre-action correspondence designed
to silence rather than to resolve as a conduct risk.

**Confidentiality in pre-action correspondence.** A letter marked "without prejudice" is protected only
if it is a genuine attempt to settle a dispute; the label alone does not create the privilege, and
labelling an open assertion of claim "without prejudice" does not make it so.

**Undertakings.** Any undertaking given in pre-action correspondence — to preserve documents, to hold
funds, not to issue before a date — is personally binding on the solicitor and enforceable by the
court. Give none that is not within your control.

## Check yourself

**Q1.** A surveyor negligently valued a property on 1 March 2018. The claimant relied on the valuation
and bought the property on 1 June 2018, suffering an immediate loss. The claimant did not discover the
negligence until 1 September 2024, when a second survey revealed it. The claimant consults a solicitor
on 1 October 2026. There is no contract under deed.

Which of the following is correct?

A. Both the contract and the tort claims are statute-barred, and no extension is available.

B. The contract claim is statute-barred, but the tortious claim may be brought under s.14A of the
Limitation Act 1980, which gives the claimant three years from the date of knowledge, expiring on
1 September 2027, subject to the 15-year longstop in s.14B.

C. Both claims remain in time, because time did not begin to run until the negligence was discovered.

D. The court may exercise its discretion under s.33 to disapply the limitation period.

E. The tortious claim is statute-barred, but the contract claim remains in time because a contract
claim runs from the date of discovery.

**Q2.** An English company sells machinery to a Spanish company. The contract contains no choice of law
clause and no jurisdiction clause. A dispute arises about whether the machinery conformed to the
contract.

Which law governs the contract?

A. Spanish law, because the buyer is Spanish and the goods were delivered there.

B. English law, because the seller has its habitual residence in England and the contract is one for
the sale of goods.

C. The law of the country with which the contract is most closely connected, which will always be that
of the place of delivery.

D. English law, because proceedings would be issued in England.

E. There is no applicable law until the parties agree one.

**Q3.** A claimant is injured in a road accident in Portugal caused by the negligent driving of another
English resident, who was also on holiday there. Both are habitually resident in England. The claimant
issues proceedings in England.

Which law applies to the tort?

A. Portuguese law, under Article 4(1) of Rome II, because that is where the damage occurred.

B. English law, under Article 4(2) of Rome II, because both parties were habitually resident in the
same country when the damage occurred.

C. English law, because the claim was issued in England and the forum applies its own law.

D. Portuguese law, because the event giving rise to the damage occurred there and Article 4(1) looks to
the place of the event.

E. The claimant may choose which law applies.

**Q4.** A claimant issues a claim for £85,000 for breach of a commercial supply contract, with no
personal injury element, in the High Court.

Which of the following is correct?

A. The claim is properly issued, because a claim for more than £50,000 may be issued in the High Court.

B. The claim should have been started in the County Court, because a money claim of £100,000 or less
may only be started there; the court may transfer it and may penalise the claimant in costs.

C. The claim is a nullity and must be reissued.

D. The claim is properly issued, because commercial claims may always be issued in the High Court.

E. The claim should have been issued in the Commercial Court.

**Q5.** A defendant fails to respond at all to a letter of claim sent under the Practice Direction on
Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols, and ignores an invitation to mediate. Proceedings are issued and the
defendant ultimately succeeds at trial.

Which of the following is the most likely consequence of the defendant's pre-action conduct?

A. The claim will be struck out for failure to comply with the Practice Direction.

B. There is no consequence, because the defendant won.

C. The court may take the non-compliance into account in exercising its discretion as to costs, and may
reduce or disallow part of the successful defendant's costs or order costs on a different basis.

D. The defendant will be ordered to pay interest at up to 10% above base rate.

E. The court must order a stay of the proceedings.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers and explanations"}

**Q1 — B.** The **contract** claim accrued on **breach** — the negligent valuation on 1 March 2018 — so
the six-year period under s.5 expired on 1 March 2024. The **tortious** claim accrued when **damage**
was suffered on 1 June 2018, so the primary six-year period under s.2 expired on 1 June 2024. But s.14A
gives the claimant the **longer** of six years from accrual and **three years from the date of
knowledge**. Knowledge came on 1 September 2024, so the claim may be brought until 1 September 2027 —
comfortably covering a consultation in October 2026. The s.14B **15-year longstop** runs from the
negligent act (1 March 2018) and does not expire until 2033.

- **A** overlooks s.14A entirely.
- **C** applies a discoverability rule to the contract claim, where none exists.
- **D** applies s.33, which is confined to **personal injury and fatal accident** claims.
- **E** reverses the position: it is the **tort** claim that benefits from the knowledge extension, not
  the contract claim.

**Q2 — B.** Rome I, Article 4(1)(a): in the absence of choice, a contract for the **sale of goods** is
governed by the law of the country where the **seller** has their habitual residence. The seller is
English, so English law applies. (For a company, habitual residence means its place of central
administration.)

- **A** applies the buyer's law, which is the opposite of the rule.
- **C** skips the specific rules in Art 4(1) and goes straight to a closest-connection test, and then
  states it inflexibly. Article 4(3) is an **escape clause** requiring a *manifestly* closer connection.
- **D** confuses jurisdiction with applicable law. An English court frequently applies foreign law.
- **E** is simply wrong: Rome I supplies the answer where the parties have not.

**Q3 — B.** Rome II, Article 4(2): where both the person claimed to be liable and the person sustaining
damage are habitually resident in the **same country** when the damage occurs, the law of that country
applies **instead of** the Art 4(1) rule. Both are habitually resident in England, so English law
governs — including on quantification of damages.

- **A** and **D** apply Art 4(1) without checking Art 4(2), and **D** additionally misstates Art 4(1),
  which looks to where the **damage** occurs, not the event.
- **C** assumes the forum applies its own law, which is what the Rome Regulations exist to prevent.
- **E** offers a unilateral choice that exists only under Art 7 (environmental damage). Article 14
  requires **agreement**.

**Q4 — B.** Practice Direction 7A: proceedings may only be **started** in the High Court if the value of
the claim exceeds **£100,000** (or, for personal injury, is £50,000 or more). £85,000 is below the
threshold, so the claim belongs in the County Court.

- **A** applies the personal injury threshold to a non-personal injury claim.
- **C** overstates the consequence: starting in the wrong court is an irregularity, not a nullity. The
  court may transfer under s.40 County Courts Act 1984.
- **D** invents a rule; the Commercial Court has its own criteria and the value here is far below what
  it would ordinarily take.
- **E** compounds the error.

**Q5 — C.** Non-compliance with the Practice Direction is taken into account in the exercise of the
court's **costs** discretion (CPR 44.2(4)(a) — conduct, including conduct before proceedings). The
court may reduce or disallow part of the successful party's costs, or award costs on the indemnity
basis against the party at fault. Ignoring an invitation to mediate compounds the point: silence in
response to such an invitation may itself be unreasonable.

- **A** overstates the sanction; failure to comply with a protocol does not invalidate or defeat a
  claim.
- **B** ignores the court's power to deprive even a **successful** party of costs for its conduct.
- **D** applies a sanction available against a **defendant ordered to pay a sum of money** — this
  defendant won and pays nothing.
- **E** describes a discretionary remedy, and one directed at incomplete protocol steps before trial,
  not at a defendant who has already succeeded.

:::
